sections.title: Current conclusion
sections.markdown: Reviewed 31 October 2026: the Calton pensioner is a leading compatible identity of the Royal Scots soldier and the Struthers Street memorial account Glasgow-2875. The original pension register records the soldier’s death on 12 January 1848. His parents remain unknown; the 1782 indexed child has no parents in the inspected index and is not proved as the adult. No merger, parent attachment, date-field change or confidence gain is selected.

sections.title: Original military identity test — 31 October 2026
sections.markdown:
The original discharge describes Sergeant John Glasgow of the 1st Battalion Royal Scots, born in the parish and town of Glasgow, Lanark, about thirty-five years old and formerly a labourer. He enlisted at eighteen; the service table begins 7 May 1800. The discharge was signed at Belfast on 10 March 1817, for hernia, and recommends Glasgow for his pension. The following sheet contains his signed receipt and the certification that the disability did not arise from misconduct. The later 1st Foot pension register records admission on 26 March 1817, residence Glasgow and death on 12 January 1848.

The regiment and March 1817 pension chronology link the two military originals. The Glasgow birthplace and pensioner status fit John Glasgow-2968, the 1841 Calton army pensioner/burgh officer at 11 Struthers Street with wife Elizabeth. His rounded census age 55 permits an early-1780s birth; the inherited 1786 is not an exact contrary birthday. Glasgow-2875 has the separately held memorial lead for a January 1848 Southern Necropolis burial and Struthers Street residence. The matching street and death month make 2875 and 2968 a particularly strong identity comparison and give a concrete route from the household to the soldier.

The originals name no father, mother, wife or children and give no Struthers Street address. Identification with the Calton household and the memorial profile remains inferred, not a completed merger. The 1848 memorial is a derivative lead without an inspected grave photograph. The 1782 indexed child attached to 2875 remains a separate unproved childhood-to-adult identification: its inspected FamilySearch entry gives only August 1782, Glasgow and no parents. No father is invented or assigned; both live profiles currently have no parents. No relationship percentage, structural attachment, birth field or death field changes, and no confidence-progress gain is counted.

Sources: [WO 119/41 original discharge front](https://search.findmypast.co.uk/record?id=GBM%2FWO119%2F0041%2F001_023&parentid=GBM%2FWO119%2F27887) · [signed continuation](https://search.findmypast.co.uk/record/browse?id=gbm%2fwo119%2f0041%2f001_024) · [WO 23/36 original pension register, printed p.26 facing p.25](https://search.findmypast.co.uk/record?id=GBM%2FWO23%2F36%2F00026&parentid=GBM%2FWO23%2F36%2F00026%2F1030358) · [1782 index X1WW-W8Z](https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1WW-W8Z). Original military scans and index inspected 31 October 2026; raw licensed scans retained privately. The military index hit already occurred in the 7 October sweep; this is a new original-record reading and identity correlation, not a newly discovered index hit.

Next useful test: Read the August 1782 Glasgow entry in the original blotter registers to recover any named parents, then compare competing local childhoods and the household. FamilySearch catalogue koha:348349 identifies film 1041382 / DGS 008075802 (baptisms 1776–1797 and 1817–1820); signed-in home access was tested and explicitly requires a FamilySearch Center or affiliate library. The index itself also cites films 908248 and 102913 and DGS 8059265; reconcile those parallel copies rather than treating every film as the same volume. Scotland’s People is excluded by the owner’s instruction. A second independent household/death record naming regiment, wife or Struthers Street would strengthen the adult match.

The [John Glasgow memorial, 245479765](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/245479765/john-glasgow) was rechecked 31 October 2026: January 1848, birth year 1783, resident of Struthers Street, zero photographs. These are derivative memorial statements, not a newly inspected burial register; the matching death month and street support the existing-profile comparison.

potential_parentage.method: Automated leads use birth surnames—not married surnames—as parental eligibility, role-specific biological age limits, bounded and approximate-date uncertainty, household chronology, specific time-aware localities, mapped distance, tenancy succession, migration destinations and sex-aware Scottish naming positions across generations. People already attached as the subject's parents stay in the identity summary and are excluded from this alternative-candidate list, regardless of relationship confidence. The main calibration uses clues available on disconnected profiles; existing parent and sibling links are retained as comparison context rather than treated as transferable evidence. Common ordered names and grandparent-to-child echoes receive a small non-zero weight, so a John or James match can support several independent criteria without producing a lead alone. Rare names, repeated bearers and bundles across otherwise distinct branches receive substantially more weight according to catalogue frequency. An exact migration place is weighted by its rarity and repetition across both branches; a shared destination country is worth only one point. Extra weight is added only when at least three independent clue types converge: naming, locality, specific migration, household chronology or collateral networks. Sparse profiles retain a clearly labelled chronology-only fallback instead of disappearing. Countries, states, counties and research clusters do not count as a shared locality, and fallback, broad representative or kin-inferred coordinates are excluded from distance scoring. Shared descendant profiles are removed before branch-name comparison. A candidate already recorded as a parent-in-law is excluded. A confident or independently supported parent is treated as settled; uncertain and unassessed attachments remain open to alternative comparison. A different linked parent, an uncle/aunt or grandparent path, and a matching existing child profile prevent an alternative from being classified as a strong direct-parent lead until the underlying tree conflict or duplicate is resolved. Familiar forms such as Bessie are normalised. Surname remains an eligibility filter worth zero points.
potential_parentage.warning: Naming customs, shared farms and occupations are circumstantial. Children, spouses and collateral relatives may be missing, and tree-derived family networks are not independent evidence. Scores rank research leads; they do not prove parentage.
